key_facts: Plaintiff applied via hiring.amazon.com for the position of XL Warehouse Associate at Amazon.com Services, LLC's fulfillment center, 44051 Osgood Rd, Fremont, CA 94539 (Alameda County). Position: $21.50–$24.00/hour (per the Jul. 3, 2026 offer letter's stated range), 19 hours/week, Seasonal; possible start date July 28, 2026. Hiring timeline: Application submitted approximately early July 2026. On July 3, 2026 (2:09 PM), Amazon Jobs emailed a conditional offer — 'Congratulations on Your Amazon Offer!' — expressly conditioned on 'successful completion of your background check, drug test, and all pre-hire activities,' with training dates set for July 28–29 and August 4–5, 2026. On July 3, 2026 (2:20 PM), Amazon Jobs confirmed the Pre-Hire Appointment for July 7, 2026 by email and matching SMS (shortcode 39816), instructing Plaintiff to complete Form I-9 in advance. Plaintiff completed Form I-9 online the evening of July 4, 2026 (system audit log session 2026-07-05T03:07–03:12 UTC; Section 1 attestation: 'An alien authorized to work,' USCIS/A-Number on file, expiration 05/12/2027); Amazon Jobs sent Pre-Hire Appointment reminder emails/SMS on July 4 (2:51 PM) and July 6 (2:53 PM, shortcode 39816). Amazon's Simple Hire checklist confirmed: Drug Test COMPLETE, I-9 Verification COMPLETE, Background Check PENDING. Pre-hire appointment attended July 7, 2026 (9:00–9:30 AM) at the onsite Recruiting Office, Amazon Distribution Center, 44051 Osgood Rd., Fremont, CA; Amazon Jobs emailed a 'Completed Pre-Hire Appointment' confirmation at 9:20 AM. On July 4, 2026, Equifax sent an onboarding-packet reminder email to Plaintiff's bnn.cdl@gmail.com account. On July 6, 2026, Amazon Jobs (shortcode 31432, 9:37 AM) texted Plaintiff explaining the four-day paid training requirement, and Amazon Workforce Staffing sent an application-experience survey email at 10:22 AM. On July 7, 2026 (9:22 AM), shortcode 45996 texted: 'Reply START to receive text messages from Accurate Background (requesting background check on behalf of Amazon).' — confirming that Accurate Background is Amazon's BGC vendor for this hiring pipeline. Plaintiff did not reply START and subscribe until July 17, 2026 (7:54 AM) — 10 days after Accurate Background's original request, the same morning as Amazon's second delay-apology email, not same-day as previously assumed. Also on July 7, 2026, Accurate Background emailed a 'Notification of Electronic Communication' formally identifying itself as 'a consumer reporting agency' retained by 'Amazon Salesforce' to complete screening Y94611404, and separately emailed an 'Other Information Needed for Screening Request' notice (search ID# 496623722) directly asking Plaintiff to call and confirm his Social Security number, prior names, address history, and date of birth as 'an urgent matter,' warning that failure to respond promptly 'will result in delays in processing your screening' — a mid-screening, manual identity-verification step consistent with a registry-name-match requiring confirmation before the BGC could be completed. On July 8, 2026, Amazon Jobs texted: 'Just an update on your background check. At the site you applied to, background checks are usually returned 5 days after they are submitted.' On July 12, 2026, Amazon Jobs emailed (noreply@jobs.amazon.com): 'Your application with Amazon is still in progress. The time to complete the background check and testing can vary, so we thank you for your patience.' On July 17, 2026 — 10 days after the BGC was ordered — Amazon Jobs emailed again: 'We are still waiting for your background check results and sincerely apologize for the delay. These background checks are processed through a third-party vendor, so we will notify you via email as soon as your results are provided to us.' As of July 27, 2026 (3:23 PM), Amazon's Simple Hire checklist still shows the Background Check as 'Pending' — 20 days after submission, with only 1 of 6 onboarding activities (the I-9) complete — and no formal adverse action notice has issued. That same checklist now reads 'You do not have a shift selected — Please select a new shift,' overwriting the specific training shift (July 28–29 and August 4–5, 2026) that the July 3 offer had locked in — one day before that training was to begin. Amazon and Accurate Background cannot indefinitely stall a hiring decision while holding the applicant in limbo: the disappearance of a confirmed, dated shift assignment on the eve of its own start date is the practical, de facto loss of the position, occurring independently of and prior to any formal FCRA/ICRAA adverse-action notice. The extended delay (20+ days vs. the stated 5-day norm, compounded by the mid-screening identity-verification request) is directly consistent with the registry-flag pattern observed across Matters 22, 25, 26, and 27: Plaintiff's California Sex Offender Registry listing triggers a hold, escalation, or adverse-recommendation status in the BGC that causes the vendor to delay or deny. Cal. Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E) is a categorical prohibition on the use of sex offender registry information for employment purposes. No exception applies to a warehouse associate position. Amazon.com Services, LLC, as the hiring employer, is prohibited from using registry information — whether directly accessed or obtained through Accurate Background — for any employment-related purpose. This is the sixth matter in the portfolio asserting the PC §290.46(j) theory (Matters 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29), though only four of those (22, 25, 26, 27) involve a confirmed adverse action to date — Matter 23's anticipated adverse action never occurred (Macy's completed the hire; see Matter 23), and this matter's own adverse action is still pending, not confirmed. PRIOR LITIGATION — CORRECTED RECORD (full docket now on file at /documents/matter-29/lerma-v-amazon/): Miguel Lerma, Jr. v. Amazon.com Services, LLC et al., Case No. 8:22-cv-01727 (C.D. Cal.), filed September 21, 2022. Lerma, a registered California sex offender under PC §290, completed a seasonal Amazon fulfillment-center assignment without incident (Nov. 2021–Mar. 2022), then separately applied for a permanent Amazon Fresh store-associate position; Accurate Background generated a background report on March 22, 2022 that led to pre-adverse (Mar. 23) and post-adverse (Apr. 6) action notices citing two 2013 felony rape convictions as 'the basis for the decision.' Lerma's First Amended Complaint (Dkt. 20, Nov. 15, 2022) pled five claims: Megan's Law/PC §290.46 (against both defendants), the California Fair Chance Act, Gov. Code §12952 (against Amazon only), ICRAA (against Accurate only), FCRA (against Accurate only), and UCL (against both). CONTRARY TO THIS MATTER'S PRIOR CHARACTERIZATION, THE MEGAN'S LAW CLAIM WAS NOT VINDICATED OR SETTLED — IT WAS DISMISSED. On May 26, 2023 (Dkt. 36), Judge Fred W. Slaughter GRANTED both defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motions and dismissed the Megan's Law, FCRA, and UCL claims without prejudice, holding that Accurate Background's own background report — subject to judicial notice — showed the disqualifying conviction information came from ordinary Orange County Superior Court criminal records, not the Megan's Law website; the report's own 'National Sex Offender Database Search' returned 'NO RECORD FOUND.' The FCRA claim failed because it was pled as entirely derivative of the (rejected) Megan's Law theory. The ICRAA claim had already been voluntarily dismissed by Lerma's own counsel, unopposed, after Accurate raised a seven-year-lookback defense. The UCL claim failed for lack of federal equitable standing (an adequate legal remedy existed). Lerma never filed the invited Second Amended Complaint; the court issued an Order to Show Cause re dismissal for lack of prosecution (Aug. 3, 2023, Dkt. 43) before Amazon answered the FAC on Aug. 23, 2023 (Dkt. 45) as to the one claim neither motion had challenged: the Fair Chance Act claim against Amazon, based on Amazon's alleged failure to individually assess Lerma's decade-old conviction against the specific duties of the store-associate role despite having previously employed and praised him. The case settled on that surviving claim on Sept. 21, 2023 (Notice of Settlement, Dkt. 46) and was dismissed without prejudice Sept. 29, 2023 (Dkt. 47); a stipulation to dismiss followed Oct. 26, 2023 (Dkt. 48). Settlement terms were not publicly disclosed. REVISED TAKEAWAYS FOR MATTER 29: (1) The Lerma settlement does NOT establish willfulness for continued Megan's Law/registry misuse specifically — that theory was rejected on this record, not proven. Any punitive-damages argument premised on 'Amazon settled the identical §290.46(j) claim' overstates the record and should not be advanced without qualification. (2) Lerma's dismissal turns on a plausibility gap this matter must close: Lerma's own background report affirmatively contradicted his registry-sourcing theory. Matter 29 needs the actual Accurate Background report — once obtained — to show whether the National Sex Offender Database Search component itself returns a hit or hold, which would meaningfully distinguish this matter from Lerma rather than merely repeating its rejected theory. (3) The Fair Chance Act claim that Amazon never contested and ultimately paid to resolve is a live, independent cause of action fitting this matter's facts (Amazon's Simple Hire process shows no individualized assessment of Plaintiff's registry status against the XL Warehouse Associate duties) and has been added to Matter 29's causes of action above. (4) Amazon and Accurate Background remain on notice of this exact litigation history and the exact background-check vendor relationship, which supports a notice/knowledge argument going to willfulness generally, short of a settled-liability admission on the registry theory specifically.

damages: Statutory civil remedy under PC § 290.46(j)(4)(A): actual damages or $25,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees, per unlawful use of registry information, plus Fair Chance Act (Gov. Code §12952) damages for failure to individually assess. Position is seasonal, part-time ($21.50/hr × 19 hrs/wk = $408.50/wk), limiting actual lost-wage recovery relative to the full-time employment matters. Statutory penalties and emotional distress (sixth cumulative registry-based denial) are the primary recovery mechanisms. CONSERVATIVE: ~$30,000 (§290.46(j)(4)(A) statutory minimum plus modest ICRAA statutory and emotional distress; Fair Chance Act claim pursued primarily for injunctive/individualized-assessment relief rather than added dollar recovery at this end of the range). MODERATE: ~$75,000 (statutory penalty; Fair Chance Act damages for the individualized-assessment failure — the one theory Amazon paid to resolve in Lerma; ICRAA willful noncompliance; emotional distress amplified by sixth cumulative denial; fee shifting). AGGRESSIVE: ~$150,000 (revised down from the prior estimate, which rested on a mischaracterized 'Amazon settled the identical §290.46(j) claim' premise — see key_facts and risk; the Lerma docket shows that claim was dismissed, not settled, so punitive damages under Civ. Code §3294 here must rest on notice/knowledge generally and on confirmation from the actual BGC report, not on an assumed prior admission; portfolio-wide pattern across six employers and Amazon's net worth still support a punitive multiplier if the registry basis is confirmed).
risk: Favorable on the Fair Chance Act claim; moderate-to-favorable but evidence-dependent on the Megan's Law/§290.46(j) claim, corrected in light of the full Lerma docket now on file. Lerma v. Amazon.com Services, LLC et al., No. 8:22-cv-01727 (C.D. Cal.), does NOT establish willfulness for registry misuse as previously stated in this record: the identical Megan's Law claim was DISMISSED on May 26, 2023 because Accurate Background's own background report contradicted the registry-sourcing theory (its National Sex Offender Database Search returned 'no record found'; the disqualifying information came from ordinary criminal court records). Only a Fair Chance Act claim against Amazon (individualized-assessment failure) survived to the September 2023 settlement. Any punitive-damages theory should rest on notice/knowledge of the litigation and vendor relationship generally, not on a false premise that Amazon 'settled the identical claim.' Principal risks at this stage: (1) a formal adverse action notice has not yet been issued, so the BGC result has not been confirmed in writing as the basis for any action; (2) without the actual BGC report (unlike Matter 27, where the InfoMart report is in hand), the registry basis is inferred from the delay pattern and the Jul. 7, 2026 mid-screening identity-verification request — Lerma is a cautionary tale that this inference can be defeated if the actual report (once obtained) shows, like Lerma's did, that the National Sex Offender Database Search came back clean and the delay has some other explanation; (3) the position is seasonal/part-time ($21.50/hr × 19 hrs/wk), limiting actual lost-wage exposure relative to Matters 22/27. Mitigating this: the Jul. 27, 2026 checklist's 'you do not have a shift selected' status — replacing the confirmed Jul. 28–29/Aug. 4–5 training shift one day before it was to begin — is concrete, dated evidence that the specific position has already been lost in practice, independent of and prior to any adverse action letter; this narrows the 'no adverse action yet' risk and supports treating the claim as ripe even absent formal notice. The Fair Chance Act claim added to this matter is independently strong regardless of how the registry theory develops: Amazon's Simple Hire process shows no individualized assessment step at all, mirroring the exact gap Amazon paid to resolve in Lerma. Once an adverse action notice is received on the §290.46(j) claim, the liability case would substantially mirror Matter 22 (Pilot) if — and only if — the actual report identifies the registry as the disqualifying factor; Lerma shows this cannot be assumed from the delay pattern alone. Amazon's $500B+ market capitalization and Accurate Background's status as a repeat background-check litigation defendant remain relevant to any punitive exposure that is otherwise established. Removal is timely federal-question (FCRA on the face of the complaint; Accurate consented). Remand is not worth filing. Expect a Rule 12(b)(6) by the September 22 extended date (Dkt. 6 / Dkt. 7); Lerma remains the caution on the registry-sourcing theory. State §425.115 sets nothing federally — FRCP 54(c) controls.
